title: Having Teachers Debate Tough Choices
author: Rod J. Naquin
summary: Naquin describes a 45-minute district PD session in which teachers picked a side on forced-choice dilemmas about teaching, such as teaching first versus letting students try first, or lunch with students versus eating alone. He builds the session on Mary Kennedy's five persistent problems of teaching and argues that these problems compete, so any strategy solves one problem while making another harder. He extends Kennedy with Dan Hudson, Harry Fletcher-Wood, Paul Kirschner and Lefstein and Snell, treating evidence-informed practice as research in service of teacher judgment. He highlights the often-omitted fifth problem, teachers' own needs, as a more coherent way to think about wellbeing. He closes with a usable talk move for debriefs, PLCs and rollouts: which problem is that solving, and what might it make harder.
points: Kennedy sorts teaching by purpose into five persistent problems, and the problems compete, so no practice is free of cost.
Forced-choice debates make reasoning visible, and showing research after teachers argue turns studies into evidence rather than verdicts.
The fifth problem, taking care of yourself, is routinely dropped from summaries but offers a better lens on workload and attrition.
The talk move 'Which problem is that solving, and what might it make harder?' turns loyalty tests about strategies into questions about a specific class and cost.
quotes: A forced choice makes people commit, and commitment makes reasoning visible.
The part of Kennedy’s argument that matters most is that these problems compete.
Clamp down on behavior and participation drops; get students excited and the room gets loud.
A doctor weighs evidence for one patient. A teacher weighs it for thirty students at once, across five problems that pull against each other.
Teachers argued first and saw the research second, so studies entered the conversation as evidence rather than verdicts.
Treating lunch as a teaching decision with real trade-offs, rather than a test of how much you care, may be the most practical thing a November PD session can offer.
Together they turn “Should we use cold call?” from a loyalty test into a question about this class and this cost.
